transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-06-15 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 58 minutes (approx)
- Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Mei (Redwood PM); Marcus (Cobalt Lead ML Platform), Sofia (Cobalt SRE), Derek (CTO), Rina (SecOps)

Summary: Priya ran through an OTLP-first tracing strategy for token-level metrics and KV cache visibility; we mapped spans to model request lifecycle, sketched attributes (token_count, kv_cache_hit, batch_size, model_version), and discussed practical collector sampling, storage costs, and dashboarding patterns. The team agreed to run a targeted benchmark and exchange config artifacts.

--- Topics / Outline ---
0:00 Intro and goals
6:20 OTLP topology and exporter choices
14:10 Token-level spans & attribute naming
24:50 KV cache telemetry and metrics cardinality concerns
34:00 Batching + tail latency tradeoffs, quantization notes
45:30 VPC/on-prem collector constraints and secrets (KMS/HSM)
53:10 Recap and next steps

--- Transcript (annotated, auto-transcribed, some artifacts) ---
00:00 Alex (Redwood AE): All right everyone we can start. Thanks for joining, we wanted to make this session very practical — a runbook, not a paper. Priya will take us through the tracing/OTLP design and then we can map to dashboards.
00:22 Priya (Redwood SE): Hi hi, quick agenda — OTLP collector placement, span design for token-level signals, KV cache metrics, batching, and finally dashboard + alerts. I'll pause often for questions.
00:37 Marcus (Cobalt): Great thanks. Our main ask: we need per-token visibility to troubleshoot p99 spikes in production; we also want to avoid huge storage bills.
00:48 Priya: Yep, that's the tension — fidelity vs cost. Two approaches: 1) token-level spans for sampled requests, with aggregate metrics for all requests (like kv_cache_hit / total_tokens), or 2) emit token metrics as aggregated histograms per request. Each has tradeoffs.
01:05 Sofia (SRE): Quick clarification — when you say token-level spans do you mean a span per token? that seems... big.
01:12 Priya: Good point. We generally recommend token-level spans only when sampling a request (say 1-5% of requests) or for tracebacks during incidents. For normal ops, attach attributes to the request span: token_count, generated_tokens, kv_hits, batch_size, quant_profile. And emit per-request histograms that capture token timing distribution.
02:00 Jordan (Redwood SE): Also, continuous batching complicates attribution — a single GPU batch can contain multiple logical requests; we model the serving path as: inbound request span -> prebatch span -> batch execution span(s) -> postprocess span. Within the batch execution span we add per-request attributes for kv_cache_hit and token_counts.
02:35 Derek (CTO): So for our model (finance summarization, variable length, sometimes 1k tokens), will the attributes be enough to isolate tail latency?
02:44 Priya: Yes if you have good histograms and p99 per token-length bucket. We recommend tagging request spans with token-length buckets (e.g., <64, 64-256, 256-1024, >1024). That lets dashboards slice p95/p99 by length.
03:12 Marcus: Ok that helps. What about cardinality? we're worried about metric explosion if we put model_version + shard + region + kv_key pattern.
03:22 Priya: Keep high-cardinality fields out of time-series metrics. Put them as span attributes only. For metrics, roll up: model_family, model_version, region, token_bucket, kv_hit_ratio. Avoid dynamic keys in metric labels.
04:10 Rina (SecOps): For on-prem, we have strict egress rules. How do we get traces off box?
04:18 Mei (Redwood PM): We often use a local OTLP collector in the customer's VPC which buffers to an internal observability cluster (Tempo/Jaeger) or we can forward to Redwood-managed observability under a private peering link. If egress is blocked, we run a collector that ships via SFTP or a secure replication lane — but that is more of a special case.
05:00 Sofia: Does Redwood's Private deployment include collector hosting?
05:06 Alex: In Private mode we provide a managed control plane but customers run a local collector that writes to the customer's observability stack or to ours across a private link. We'll share a sample runbook for both patterns.
06:20 Priya: Ok switching to OTLP topology. Two patterns: edge collectors (per cluster) vs centralized collector cluster. Edge collectors reduce latency but increase management. Centralized collector simplifies config but can introduce backpressure. For token-level traces we prefer edge collectors with local sampling and batching to avoid network spikes.
07:05 Marcus: What's the recommended sampling policy? we need to catch anomalies but not blow up storage.
07:12 Priya: Start with adaptive sampling: sample 0.5-1% baseline, increase sampling to 10% for requests with kv_cache_miss or batch_size > threshold or high latency. We emit aggregated metrics for all requests so you still get full signals for dashboards.
08:00 Jordan: Implementation detail — set a sampled_tag if kv_cache_miss==true, or if token_bucket==">1024" then force sample with probability X. This reduces the chance we miss long-tail cases.
09:05 Sofia: How do you compute kv_cache_hit metrics? do you emit a counter per hit per token?
09:12 Priya: We recommend counting per-request: kv_hits (int), kv_lookups (int), and emit kv_hit_ratio = kv_hits/kv_lookups as a gauge. That avoids per-token counters. For debugging traces we keep kv_key patterns in the span attributes but scrub sensitive keys.
10:00 Marcus: Are there PII concerns with span attributes? we have token contents, sometimes customer PII in prompts.
10:10 Priya: Yes, scrub sensitive content. Store token_count and token_types but not token text. Use a policy to hash or redact prompt text and send only metadata. Redwood supports redaction filters in the collector. We'll share config.
11:30 Derek: Let's talk dashboards. What should our Grafana look like?
11:38 Priya: Core dashboards: 1) Request-level overview (throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate), 2) Token-level efficiency (tokens/sec, avg tokens/request, p95 token-gen time), 3) KV cache dashboard (hit ratio over time, per-model hit ratio), 4) Batch telemetry (batch size distribution, queue wait time), 5) Incident drill-down (sampled traces with token histograms). We'll attach a starter JSON.
13:20 Marcus: Could you show a concrete example of a span for a batched request?
13:28 Priya: Sure — top-level span: request.id, attributes: model_version, token_count, token_bucket, kv_hit_ratio, quant_profile. Prebatch span: prebatch.queue_time_ms. Batch exec span: batch_size, gpu_exec_ms, per_request_index. Postproc span: token_emit_time_ms. Sampled child spans: token_emit_{i} only for sampled traces.
15:10 Jordan: Note — per_request_index helps map slices of the GPU batch to original requests for trace visualization.
16:02 Sofia: About storage — if we keep metrics and sampled traces, what's the ballpark cost?
16:08 Priya: Rough back-of-envelope: metrics and aggregated histograms are cheap; sampled traces vary. If you sample 1% with average trace size ~20KB, for 1000 rps that's ~17GB/day. Use 0.5% and local pre-aggregation (span compression) to lower it. We can run a short benchmark to give concrete numbers.
17:40 Marcus: Ok let's schedule that. Next, batching: we see p99 spikes when batch sizes suddenly grow. Any mitigations?
18:00 Priya: Two levers: dynamic batching policy that caps max_wait_ms and max_batch_size and preemptive routing for latency-sensitive requests (route to a low-latency pool without batching). Also prioritize prefix caching and KV caching to avoid regeneration. On traces, emit queue_time and batch_size to correlate spikes.
19:05 Derek: Quantization — we're exploring 4-bit to reduce GPU memory, any observability impact?
19:18 Priya: Quantization can change per-token latency (model exec faster) but sometimes increases variance. Add quant_profile attribute (e.g., q4_0, int8) to request spans so you can slice latency by quantization. Watch for degradation in output quality; Redwood Optimize has eval hooks we can integrate.
20:25 Rina: For on-prem / VPC, about secrets: KMS/HSM — do collectors need to access keys?
20:34 Alex: No, collectors should not have application keys. Use short-lived credentials and a secrets agent. For HSM you can keep signing done by a local key manager and export only non-sensitive telemetry. We'll include recommended IAM roles in the runbook.
21:10 Marcus: What about alerting thresholds?
21:18 Priya: Alert on increases in kv_miss_ratio above baseline, sustained p99 above SLA, and sudden increase in batch_queue_time. Use anomaly detection on histograms rather than fixed thresholds for token-heavy workloads.
22:05 Sofia: Any pitfalls when integrating Jaeger/Tempo with OTLP?
22:12 Jordan: The main issues are sampler config mismatches and attribute mapping. Make sure the collector preserves span IDs and parent relationships. For Tempo you want a consistent TraceID schema. Also be careful with label cardinality in Loki/Grafana.
23:45 Marcus: Can Redwood provide a starter OTLP collector config?
23:50 Priya: Yes — action item. We'll send a collector config (edge collector example) with sampling rules, redaction processors, and exporters for Tempo and a metrics backend.
24:30 Derek: During incidents, we sometimes need full-fidelity traces for a short window. How do we ramp sampling up safely?
24:45 Priya: Use control-plane hooks to change sampling policy dynamically, or have a toggle (SRE-run) that increases sampling to 100% for a while and streams to a hardened storage pipeline. Remember to redact on the fly.
26:00 Sofia: For batch attribution, we need to join traces with our request IDs in logs. Recommendation?
26:08 Jordan: Use a stable request.id attribute present in logs and spans; ensure your log pipeline includes that as a label. Then you can link in Grafana via Log Links.
27:10 Marcus: A weird thing we saw: kv_cache_hit true but still high latency. Any ideas?
27:18 Priya: Could be cache eviction thrash or remote KV store latency. Add kv_lookup_latency_ms and backend_io_ms attributes. Also track kv_key_size or pattern to identify hot keys.
28:40 Derek: For on-prem private deployment, will Redwood need network access to our observability?
28:48 Alex: Two options — private peering to Redwood observability or you host the dashboards and we provide collector configs. We'll help with the peering setup as part of the workshop.
30:00 Marcus: Can we get an example dashboard that slices p99 by token_bucket and quant_profile?
30:08 Priya: Yes — that'll be in the starter JSON.
31:15 Sofia: How do we avoid exposing sensitive identifiers in span attributes?
31:22 Priya: Redaction processor — replace GUIDs with hashed tokens, and avoid sending raw prompt or user IDs. For compliance we'll provide a mapping for what should never leave the VPC.
33:00 Jordan: A couple operational notes — buffer sizes on the collector need tuning; too small and you drop spans during spikes, too large and you blow memory. We'll include recommended values per rps.
34:00 Marcus: Any advice on correlating token-level cost to spend?
34:08 Priya: Instrument token-per-second and cost-per-1k-tokens metrics and join with request throughput. Redwood Console also provides token-level cost breakdowns per model/route. We'll show that in the next session.
35:45 Derek: One last thing — we run a compliance audit next quarter. What docs can you provide?
35:52 Alex: We can provide SOC2 artifact examples, redaction config, and an architecture diagram for the collector path. Rina we'll loop you in.
36:30 Priya: Quick demo — shared screen showing sample Grafana layout (note: transcript redacts screenshots). We highlight panels: p99 by token_bucket, kv_hit_ratio heatmap, batch_size distribution, sampled traces pane.
40:20 Sofia: This is helpful. For the benchmark, what inputs do you need?
40:28 Priya: Sample load profile (rps), token-length distribution CSV, model artifact identifier, and whether KV is local or remote. Marcus to provide.
41:12 Marcus: Will do. Also include a short how-to for running a short 2-hour workload with Redwood SE on call.
41:20 Alex: We'll schedule that.
42:05 Priya: A note on quantization again — sometimes int8 reduces variance more than 4-bit depending on the model. Keep quant_profile as a slice in dashboards.
43:40 Marcus: Any gotchas with batch preemption?
43:47 Jordan: Preemption can cause reorder; ensure request IDs and per_request_index preserve ordering for debugging. Also watch for KV cache warming when you split traffic.
45:00 Rina: Security question — do we have logs of config changes for the collectors?
45:06 Alex: Yes, collectors can be run with config management (gitops) and we keep audit logs; we'll provide the GitHub examples and recommended RBAC.
46:30 Sofia: Can we see a sample alert rule for kv_miss_ratio?
46:38 Priya: Example alert: kv_miss_ratio > 0.15 sustained for 5m OR delta(kv_miss_ratio, 5m) > 0.05. Also create a paging rule that only triggers on sustained p99 SLA breaches.
48:00 Marcus: Perfect. Any questions from Redwood side?
48:06 Jordan: Just to confirm — Cobalt will share token distribution CSV and a small test vector set. We'll use that to run the benchmark and calibrate sampling.
48:20 Marcus: Yes we'll send that by end of day Friday.
49:00 Alex: Ok let's recap next steps.
49:07 Priya: Action items: send collector config, Grafana JSON, run benchmark with SE on call, schedule VPC workshop.
49:20 Marcus: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
49:28 Derek: Appreciate it.
49:30 Alex: Thanks all — we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
49:35 (call ends)
